title: AI strategy that assigns decisions, ownership, and limits before implementation.
summary: Aloha AI helps leaders determine where AI belongs, what evidence and governance the work requires, who remains accountable, and which initiatives should be designed, piloted, stopped, or scaled.
audience: Founders, executives, legal and compliance leaders, program owners, and institutions managing consequential AI adoption.
timeline: Systems Audit in about 2 weeks; architecture and implementation scopes follow the validated priorities.
fit: AI activity is scattered across teams
Leadership cannot distinguish experiments from durable operating systems
Consequential workflows require explicit review and ownership
methodology: Separate deterministic rules from generative work
assumptions: Access is provided to representative workflows and source materials
limitations: Strategy does not replace licensed legal, medical, tax, clinical, privacy, or security advice
Recommendations remain dependent on source quality and organizational participation

title: Primary-source intelligence built to survive updates, conflict, and scrutiny.
summary: Aloha AI designs research engines that discover, verify, compare, classify, monitor, and maintain legal, regulatory, scientific, market, opportunity, and institutional information.
audience: Teams whose decisions depend on changing, fragmented, or difficult-to-verify information.
deliverables: Decision briefs, dashboards, or maintained datasets
timeline: Initial architecture commonly takes 2–4 weeks; monitored systems require an agreed review and maintenance cadence.
fit: Decision makers need traceable evidence rather than summaries alone
methodology: Define the question and source hierarchy
Publish maintained outputs with review dates
assumptions: Primary sources are available or discoverable
The organization agrees on the decisions the intelligence must support
limitations: No monitor guarantees immediate detection of every change
Interpretation remains bounded by the retrieved evidence and defined jurisdiction or domain

title: Legal AI workflows where verification and professional judgment are part of the architecture.
summary: Aloha AI designs bounded research, drafting, review, intake, and knowledge workflows with source controls, permissions, approval gates, evaluation, and accountable attorney supervision where required.
audience: Law firms, legal departments, legal-technology teams, and regulated organizations improving legal work without treating model output as authority.
timeline: A bounded workflow can be diagnosed and architected in 2–4 weeks; implementation depends on systems, permissions, and supervision requirements.
fit: The team repeats research or drafting work
Citation and confidentiality failures carry material consequences
Attorneys need reviewable assistance rather than autonomous legal judgment
evidence: Controlling authority and approved research systems
methodology: Define the legal task and prohibited model roles
Evaluate against realistic matters before expansion
assumptions: A licensed attorney controls legal judgment and supervision where required
Confidentiality and system-access requirements are defined
limitations: Aloha AI does not provide legal advice or create an attorney-client relationship
No AI output should be filed, sent, or relied upon without the review required by the responsible professional

title: The Regulated Trust Stack
summary: A six-layer operating framework for evidence, compliance, production, persuasion, distribution, and defense in regulated and institutionally sensitive markets.
audience: Organizations whose public claims, internal workflows, and AI-assisted production must remain inspectable and defensible.
implementationStatus: Framework and component pages are public; individual tools vary from research concept to working beta.
roadmap: Publish versioned evidence and method registries
Add licensing and institutional implementation packages
changelog: 2026-07: component routes and public documentation consolidated
licensing: Available for institutional adaptation, implementation partnerships, and defined licensing scopes.
evidence: Primary authorities and source registers for each component
methodology: Identify the consequential claim or workflow
assumptions: Each component is configured for the relevant jurisdiction and use case
limitations: The framework is not a substitute for licensed advice
Component maturity and coverage differ and must be inspected before use

title: Aloha AI University
summary: Free foundations, practical lessons, assessments, playbooks, templates, courses, and continuing education that explain the same methods used across Aloha AI consulting, products, research, and tools.
audience: People and institutions that want to understand, evaluate, govern, and operate AI systems before or alongside implementation.
evidence: Demonstrated Aloha AI methods and builds
methodology: Begin with the learner's decision or workflow
Connect learning to tools, services, and implementation
assumptions: Learners apply professional guidance appropriate to their context
Courses and tools identify their own prerequisites and maturity
limitations: Educational content is not professional advice
Platform features, course availability, and continuing-education approval may vary
